title: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
summary: 3Blue1Brown's first chapter on deep learning explains what neurons and layers are and the math underlying a basic neural network, using handwritten digit recognition with visual animations.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.
contexts: mlabonne/llm-course: - 3Blue1Brown - But what is a Neural Network?: This video gives an intuitive explanation of neural networks and their inner workings.

title: DON'T PANIC — Hans Rosling showing the facts about population
summary: Hans Rosling uses data and animated statistics to show how world population is changing, why birth rates fall as child survival and wealth rise, and why population is expected to peak around 11 billion. It also tackles common misconceptions about Africa and family planning.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it to counter overpopulation alarm with data on falling birth rates.

title: Lecture 1 | Machine Learning (Stanford)
summary: The first lecture of Andrew Ng's Stanford CS229 Machine Learning course, giving an overview of the course. It introduces supervised and unsupervised learning, learning theory and reinforcement learning.
why_hn: Recommended as the rigorous, math-heavy original course, deeper than the Coursera version, for learning machine learning.

title: The essence of calculus
summary: The first video of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Calculus series, which builds toward integrals, derivatives, and the fundamental theorem of calculus from a simple geometry question. It aims to make viewers feel they could have invented calculus themselves.
why_hn: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.

title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
summary: Andrej Karpathy builds a GPT from scratch in code, following Attention Is All You Need and GPT-2/3, in about two hours using PyTorch. He connects it to ChatGPT and assumes familiarity with his earlier makemore videos.
why_hn: It is the go-to recommendation for learning how transformers and LLMs actually work, praised for its clarity and Karpathy's teaching.
contexts: karpathy/nn-zero-to-hero: - YouTube video lecture. For all other links see the video description.
mlabonne/llm-course: * nanoGPT by Andrej Karpathy: A 2h-long YouTube video to reimplement GPT from scratch (for programmers). He also made a video about tokenization.
Hannibal046/Awesome-LLM: - Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.

title: The determinant | Chapter 6, Essence of linear algebra
summary: A 10-minute 3Blue1Brown chapter explaining the determinant as the factor by which a linear transformation scales area or volume. It builds the idea geometrically with animations before any formulas.
why_hn: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest visual intuition for determinants, often saying it finally made the concept click.

title: Why Would AI Want to do Bad Things? Instrumental Convergence
summary: Robert Miles explains instrumental convergence: why an AGI with almost any goal would tend to pursue sub-goals like self-preservation and resource acquisition. It builds on Omohundro's basic AI drives and his orthogonality thesis video.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the clearest introduction to why smart AI might behave badly by default.

title: I don't like notebooks.- Joel Grus (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Joel Grus's JupyterCon talk explaining why he dislikes Jupyter notebooks. He covers hidden state, trouble with reproducibility and testing, and how notebooks frustrate teaching. He shows his preferred workflow and what Jupyter could change.
why_hn: It is the go-to funny, irreverent critique of notebooks, linked whenever HN debates notebooks versus testable code.

title: Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #101
summary: Lex Fridman has a three-hour conversation with Joscha Bach about artificial consciousness, the workings of the mind, intelligence and the possibly simulated nature of reality.
why_hn: Praised as a long but rewarding conversation, with commenters especially liking Bach's emphasis on modelling as a skill and his bridge between mind and computation.

title: Emacs + org-mode + python in reproducible research; SciPy 2013 Presentation
summary: John Kitchin shows how Emacs org-mode with Python lets researchers combine narrative, math, figures and executable code in one document. It exports to LaTeX, HTML and PDF, and he used it for papers and e-books.
why_hn: Repeatedly recommended as the canonical demo of org-mode for literate programming and reproducible research.

title: JPEG DCT, Discrete Cosine Transform (JPEG Pt2)- Computerphile
summary: Mike Pound explains the discrete cosine transform and how it underpins JPEG compression. It is part two of Computerphile's JPEG series.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an easy, clear intro to the DCT that finally made it click for several commenters.

title: Taking Vector Transposes Seriously | Jiahao Chen | JuliaCon 2017
summary: Jiahao Chen's JuliaCon 2017 talk argues that vector transposes should be taken seriously in type systems and linear algebra libraries. It explains why treating vectors as matrices causes trouble in languages.
why_hn: Strongly recommended for anyone working with vectors for its clear take on how they should be treated in types.

title: Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned — Kenneth Stanley
summary: A long Machine Learning Street Talk interview with Kenneth Stanley, creator of NEAT and novelty search, about his book on why greatness cannot be planned. They discuss open-endedness, the tyranny of objectives, serendipity and the evolution of ideas.
why_hn: Recommended to people who find it inspiring or perspective-changing on pursuing goals, open-ended search and AI beyond optimization.

title: [JSConfUS 2013] Steven Wittens: Making WebGL Dance
summary: Steven Wittens' JSConf US 2013 talk on drawing with WebGL, using animated visuals to walk through vectors, matrices and the rendering pipeline. Despite the title, it works as a visual primer on the linear algebra behind 3D graphics.
why_hn: HN treats it as one of the best intros to the math of 3D graphics and a staple answer to how to learn graphics programming.

title: Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4
summary: Sebastien Bubeck presents the Sparks of AGI paper at MIT, showing early experiments with GPT-4 across many domains and asking whether artificial intelligence has arrived. It includes the TikZ unicorn example.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.

title: Preface | MIT Calculus Revisited: Single Variable Calculus
summary: The preface to Herb Gross's MIT OpenCourseWare 'Calculus Revisited: Single Variable Calculus', an older black-and-white lecture series. It introduces his approach to teaching calculus from the basics.
why_hn: HN recommends Herb Gross as an unusually clear teacher whose explanations make calculus click for people who struggled elsewhere.

title: But what is a Fourier series?  From heat flow to drawing with circles | DE4
summary: 3Blue1Brown introduces Fourier series, from the heat equation to drawing arbitrary shapes with rotating circles. It builds a visual intuition for decomposing functions into sine waves.
why_hn: Recommended as the visual explanation that makes Fourier series and transforms click, even for laypeople.

title: GDC 2018: John McDonald (Valve) - Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in CSGO
summary: A GDC 2018 talk by Valve's John McDonald on VACNet, a deep learning system that analyzes CS:GO gameplay to detect cheaters. It covers how the model is trained on human-reviewed Overwatch cases and how its output feeds human moderation.
why_hn: HN points to it as the definitive example of server-side, behavioral, non-invasive anti-cheat using machine learning, often as a counterpoint to kernel-level anti-cheat.

title: But what are Hamming codes? The origin of error correction
summary: 3Blue1Brown's discovery-oriented introduction to error correction codes, building up Hamming codes from the puzzle of locating a flipped bit. It explains the parity-check idea and why it is so efficient.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an invaluable, intuitive explanation of Hamming codes that pairs well with hardware-oriented treatments.

title: The Simple Essence of Automatic Differentiation - Conal Elliott
summary: Conal Elliott presents his paper on automatic differentiation, deriving a simple, generalized AD algorithm from a natural specification. Varying the representation of derivatives yields forward and reverse mode algorithms that avoid the complexity and statefulness of backpropagation.
why_hn: Cited as the more accessible companion to the paper, and as the most interesting treatment of AD via compiling to categories.

title: 36C3 -  BahnMining - Pünktlichkeit ist eine Zier - english translation
summary: David Kriesel's 36C3 talk, in an English translation, analyzes a year of scraped Deutsche Bahn data covering every stop of every long-distance train in Germany. It explores delays and how punctuality is actually measured.
why_hn: HN brings it up in any thread about German or European rail as a data-driven, entertaining analysis of why trains are late.

title: Sci-Fi Short Film “Slaughterbots” | DUST
summary: Slaughterbots is a short sci-fi film in which swarms of cheap autonomous drones are programmed to kill targets by profile. It was made as arms-control advocacy against autonomous weapons.
why_hn: HN keeps citing it whenever drone swarms, autonomous weapons or AI warfare come up, as a believable depiction of where this leads.

title: The Most Underrated Algorithm
summary: Veritasium tells the story of the Fast Fourier Transform, from its use in detecting nuclear tests to Cold War politics, and how it could have changed the arms race. It includes a short, intuitive explanation of what the Fourier transform does.
why_hn: HN points people to it as the explanation that finally made Fourier transforms and the FFT click, with a good historical story.

title: KEYNOTE / Robert Erdmann
summary: Robert Erdmann, a materials scientist at the Rijksmuseum, gives a PyCon keynote on the ultra-high-resolution imaging of Rembrandt's Night Watch. He covers the automated gantry camera system, the Python software that drives it, and the large volumes of image data involved.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a technically jaw-dropping talk, and it is the standard reference whenever the Night Watch gigapixel images come up.

title: A visual guide to Bayesian thinking
summary: Julia Galef uses pictures to explain Bayes' rule, then tells three personal stories showing how she applies it to improve her thinking.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short, accessible intro to Bayesian reasoning and priors.

title: Playing to Lose: AI and "Civilization" (Soren Johnson)
summary: Soren Johnson, a lead designer and AI programmer on Civilization games, discusses game AI design, including whether AI should cheat, behave like a human or be fun rather than strong. He uses the Civilization series as a case study.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as the key talk on why game AI is built to be fun rather than to win.

title: Lecture 1 | Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
summary: The first lecture of Stanford's Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning course, taught by Chris Manning and Richard Socher. It introduces NLP and word vectors, including SVD, skip-gram, CBOW, negative sampling and word2vec.
why_hn: Recommended as one of the best free courses for learning modern deep learning for NLP.

title: State of GPT | BRK216HFS
summary: Andrej Karpathy walks through how GPT assistants are trained, from tokenization and pretraining to supervised finetuning and RLHF, and gives practical prompting strategies and a view of the tooling ecosystem.
why_hn: Recommended as the clearest overview of how LLM assistants are built and how to use them well.

title: 35C3 -  The Ghost in the Machine
summary: Joscha Bach's 35C3 talk offers an AI perspective on the soul, covering perception, mental representation, agency, consciousness and selfhood as things that can arise in a computational system like the brain.
why_hn: HN commenters call it lucid and fluff-free, and point to Bach as one of the most interesting voices on AI, consciousness and philosophy.

title: [CVPR'21 WAD] Keynote - Andrej Karpathy, Tesla
summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, gives a CVPR 2021 workshop keynote on how Autopilot's neural networks work. A large part covers the move to a vision-only stack, including why radar was dropped and how vision produces depth estimates.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it in Tesla threads as the primary-source explanation of why Tesla removed radar and how its vision depth estimation works.

title: Efficient Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo -- Michael Betancourt (Part 1)
summary: Michael Betancourt's lecture at MLSS Iceland 2014 on efficient Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. It covers MCMC concepts and motivation and the problems of sampling in high-dimensional distributions.
why_hn: HN people return to it as a clear primer on MCMC and HMC and on why high dimensions behave counterintuitively.

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Information Theory
summary: The first lecture of David MacKay's Cambridge course on information theory, pattern recognition and neural networks. It introduces the core ideas of his book Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms.
why_hn: Recommended as an enjoyable, clear introduction to information theory that pairs well with MacKay's free textbook.

title: You've (Likely) Been Playing The Game Of Life Wrong
summary: Veritasium explains why many real-world systems follow power laws rather than normal distributions. It covers self-organized criticality, with simulations of sandpiles, magnetism and forest fires.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for changing how they think about distributions and for showing how criticality shows up across earthquakes, wildfires and other fields.

title: CS480/680 Lecture 19: Attention and Transformer Networks
summary: A university lecture from CS480/680 by Pascal Poupart on attention mechanisms and transformer networks, worked through on a chalkboard.
why_hn: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting! - Computerphile
summary: A Computerphile video in which Dr Mike Pound and PhD student Lewis Stuart explain 3D Gaussian splatting, a quick technique that turns photos of a scene into a 3D model without much compute. It includes a demo and compares the approach to NeRFs.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Gaussian splats, made by people who understand the subject.

title: I tried using AI. It scared me.
summary: Tom Scott describes trying ChatGPT to fix his Gmail labels and being unsettled by how capable it was. He argues that we cannot know where we are on the technology curve, comparing it to Napster.
why_hn: HN cites it for the argument that we cannot tell whether AI is early or late on its sigmoid curve until hindsight.

title: Chris Lattner: Future of Programming and AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #381
summary: Lex Fridman's long podcast conversation with Chris Lattner, creator of Swift, LLVM and MLIR and co-founder of Modular. Topics include the Mojo language, the future of programming and AI, and hardware.
why_hn: HN points to it as the main place to hear Lattner's motivations and design ideas for Mojo, often in Mojo threads.

title: Introduction to Julia - Part 1 | SciPy 2014 | David Sanders
summary: David Sanders gives the first part of a two-part introduction to the Julia programming language at SciPy 2014. It walks through the language's basics and its appeal for scientific computing.
why_hn: HN commenters point newcomers to it as a solid starting point for getting to know Julia.

title: Manipulating the YouTube Algorithm - (Part 1/3) Smarter Every Day 213
summary: Part 1 of Smarter Every Day's three-part series on manipulating the YouTube algorithm. It features Renee DiResta and examples of how social media platforms can be manipulated.
why_hn: Referenced in threads on social media manipulation and junk content as an interesting miniseries, though one commenter criticized its ExpressVPN ad read.

title: Beware online "filter bubbles" | Eli Pariser
summary: Eli Pariser's TED talk argues that personalized web services trap users in filter bubbles, limiting exposure to challenging information. He says this is bad for individuals and for democracy.
why_hn: Cited as an early, prescient warning about algorithmic personalization, echo chambers and social media feeds.

title: Sacha Arnoud, Director of Engineering, Waymo - MIT Self-Driving Cars
summary: Sacha Arnoud, Waymo's Director of Engineering, gives a lecture in MIT's 2018 deep learning for self-driving cars course on the rise of machine learning in autonomous vehicles. It covers how Waymo uses deep learning and how it handles tricky driving situations.
why_hn: Pointed to during self-driving news threads as an insider view of Waymo's progress, deep learning's role and its limits.

title: Tesla AI Day 2022
summary: Tesla's full AI Day 2022 presentation, covering the Tesla Bot hardware and software, Full Self-Driving planning and perception, the occupancy network, data labeling, simulation and Dojo training infrastructure.
why_hn: HN uses it as primary-source evidence on how Tesla's vision-based driving stack and training pipeline work.

title: Bringing the Unix Philosophy to Big Data by Bryan Cantrill: FutureStack13
summary: Bryan Cantrill presents Manta, an object store with in-situ compute that lets tools like grep, awk, and sed run map-reduce style over huge data. He frames it as bringing the Unix philosophy to big data.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an elegant argument for simple Unix tools replacing heavyweight Hadoop-style pipelines.

title: Why is this number everywhere?
summary: Veritasium explores why the number 37 turns up so often, drawing on Tom Magliery's collection of 37 sightings and a poll of about 200,000 people asked to pick a random number. It covers how humans choose numbers and why 37 stands out.
why_hn: HN cites it in LLM randomness and number-picking threads as evidence that humans are also biased and predictable when asked for random numbers.

title: Stanford Seminar - Unethical Algorithms of Massive Scale
summary: Psychologist Robert Epstein presents a Stanford EE380 colloquium on how internet algorithms such as search rankings can manipulate opinions, purchases and votes at massive scale. He also describes a new monitoring system for tracking such influence.
why_hn: Cited in threads about search bias, election influence and big-tech data practices as the most comprehensive video of Epstein's research.

title: Andrew Ng: Artificial Intelligence is the New Electricity
summary: Andrew Ng speaks at the Stanford MSx Future Forum about how AI is transforming industry after industry, comparing its impact to electricity. The talk also touches on evil-AI worries, jobs and basic income.
why_hn: Recommended as a broad, practical view of AI's near-term impact from a leading practitioner, with his argument that worrying about evil AI is premature.

title: Why Asimov's Laws of Robotics Don't Work - Computerphile
summary: Rob Miles explains for Computerphile why simple rule sets like Asimov's Three Laws cannot make robots and AI safe. Terms like harm and human are too ambiguous to specify precisely.
why_hn: Pointed to in AI safety debates as a short explanation of why encoding human values as simple rules is so hard.

title: The 100 Year Flood Is Not What You Think It Is (Maybe)
summary: Practical Engineering explains what a 100-year flood actually means, combining statistics, hydrology and how society treats risk. Grady walks through local drainage infrastructure and the caveats in estimating flood probability.
why_hn: HN points to it as a clear explanation of what flood return periods really mean.

title: 🏆Award Winning🏆 CGI 3D Animated Short Film: "LAST DAY OF WAR" by Dima Fedotov | TheCGBros
summary: Last Day of War is an award-winning CGI animated short by Dima Fedotov in which automated machines keep following orders and prepare a bomber after all humans are dead.
why_hn: HN cites it in threads on military AI as a vivid depiction of where autonomous warfare could lead.

title: "Cursorless: A spoken language for editing code" by Pokey Rule (Strange Loop 2023)
summary: Pokey Rule presents Cursorless, a spoken language designed for editing code by voice, built on tree-sitter parsing with smart structural and simple token-level primitives. The talk is from Strange Loop 2023.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the best overview of Cursorless, likened to vim with your voice, and relevant to accessibility and voice coding discussions.

title: MENACE: the pile of matchboxes which can learn
summary: Matt Parker of Stand-up Maths demonstrates MENACE, Donald Michie's 1961 machine made of matchboxes that learns to play noughts and crosses through reinforcement. He builds and trains a physical version.
why_hn: HN cites it as a fun, tangible way to teach machine learning, including to kids.

title: AI Learns Noise Filtering For Photorealistic Videos | Two Minute Papers #215
summary: A Two Minute Papers episode on NVIDIA's recurrent denoising autoencoder, which cleans up noisy Monte Carlo path-traced image sequences. It shows how a neural network can produce usable renders from very few samples.
why_hn: Cited as an accessible explanation of AI denoising, which underpins real-time ray tracing on RTX hardware.

title: Do these scatter plots reveal fraudulent vote-switching in Michigan?
summary: Matt Parker of Stand-up Maths examines scatter plots that were claimed to show fraudulent vote-switching in Michigan's 2020 election. He recreates the analysis and shows that the pattern arises from comparing percentages across different bases, not from fraud.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a clear debunking of election-fraud statistics and as a warning against comparing percentages without context.

title: My Video Went Viral. Here's Why
summary: Veritasium's Derek Muller explains his hypothesis that YouTube's algorithm, not viewer preference, drives views, and that click-through rate has become the key metric. He argues this pushes creators toward clickable titles and thumbnails and leads to burnout.
why_hn: Cited in threads about recommendation algorithms and clickbait as a creator's inside view of why optimizing for click-through rate shapes content.

title: [4k, 60 fps] A Trip Through New York City in 1911
summary: Footage shot in New York City in 1911 by a Swedish film company, upscaled to 4K and 60 fps with neural networks and optionally colorized. The creator notes the colors are artificial and added only for ambiance.
why_hn: HN points to it as an impressive example of ML-based video restoration, and as the test case in the debate over whether upscaling historical footage is respectful or misleading.

title: OpenAI's GPT-4 Discussion with Red Teamer Nathan Labenz and Erik Torenberg
summary: A podcast episode in which GPT-4 red teamer Nathan Labenz describes using the model before release, finding it human-level but not human-like, and discussing its weaknesses and worrying capabilities. It closes with speculation about GPT-5.
why_hn: Cited as a firsthand account of the raw, unfiltered GPT-4 before safety tuning, especially the part after 45 minutes.

title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence | John Searle | Talks at Google
summary: John Searle's Talk at Google on consciousness and artificial intelligence, hosted by Google's Singularity Network. He presents his philosophy of mind and Chinese room argument that computation is syntactic and cannot capture semantics.
why_hn: Used as a source for Searle's own argument in Chinese room discussions, though some find nothing new in it.

title: Jonathan Diegelman - Modeling Spacecraft Separation Dynamics in Julia
summary: A JuliaCon talk by a NASA Launch Services Program engineer on modeling spacecraft separation dynamics in Julia. He describes replacing a Simulink-based workflow for checking launch vehicle separation requirements with Julia and ModelingToolkit, with large speedups and much shorter code.
why_hn: Cited again and again as the concrete case study behind the claim that NASA got a 15,000x speedup moving from Simulink to Julia.

title: ChatGPT with Rob Miles - Computerphile
summary: Computerphile interviews AI safety researcher Rob Miles about ChatGPT: how it was trained with human feedback, why it tends to produce confident nonsense, and where it may or may not be dangerous.
why_hn: HN commenters send it to people confused about ChatGPT's quirks, explaining how human-feedback training makes it a pleasing yes-man that bullshits.

title: 'Fastware' - Andrei Alexandrescu [ ACCU 2016 ]
summary: Andrei Alexandrescu's ACCU 2016 talk previews material from his book on writing fast code, with a focus on optimization techniques such as sentinels and faster search.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a careful, entertaining talk on low-level optimization that shows how textbook algorithms can be sped up.

title: Some light quantum mechanics (with minutephysics)
summary: 3Blue1Brown, in collaboration with minutephysics, introduces the math of superposition and quantum states using polarized light. It builds up the quantum behavior of photons as a simple counting and probability problem.
why_hn: Recommended as an approachable way to understand the quantum nature of light and basic quantum math without heavy machinery.

title: Survivor Bias
summary: A Veritasium video on survivor bias, explaining how an observed sample can be incomplete and skewed. It uses examples such as bombers and famous success stories.
why_hn: HN uses it as a handy reference whenever a thread needs to point at survivorship bias.

title: The mathematics of love | Hannah Fry
summary: Mathematician Hannah Fry's TED talk on patterns in dating and mate-seeking, including optimal stopping and three math-backed tips for finding a partner.
why_hn: Mentioned whenever the optimal stopping or secretary problem comes up in relation to choosing a partner.

title: The Lighthill debate on Artificial Intelligence: "The general purpose robot is a mirage"
summary: The full 1973 BBC Lighthill debate on artificial intelligence, featuring James Lighthill, Donald Michie, Richard Gregory and John McCarthy. It documents the argument that preceded the 1970s AI winter and includes early robot demos.
why_hn: HN cites it as primary-source history of AI hype and skepticism, and for the vintage Freddy robot footage.

title: Yann Lecun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #416
summary: Lex Fridman's long podcast interview with Yann LeCun on Meta AI, open source, the limits of LLMs, AGI and the future of AI.
why_hn: Cited for LeCun's views on LLM limits and alternative approaches to intelligence.

title: Can we build AI without losing control over it? | Sam Harris
summary: Sam Harris argues in a TED talk that we will build superhuman AI and have not grappled with the risk of creating something that may treat us the way we treat ants. He makes a logical case for taking AI risk seriously.
why_hn: HN cites it in AI risk debates, sometimes as an argument that has aged well and sometimes as an example of alarmist framing.

title: Deep Visualization Toolbox
summary: A short demo of the Deep Visualization Toolbox, which shows the activations inside a convolutional neural network as it processes live camera input. Viewers see individual units responding to edges, faces and text.
why_hn: HN points to it as an intuitive way to see what hidden layers of a convnet learn, and as a reference for hierarchical feature learning.

title: How We Prevent the AI’s from Killing us with Paul Christiano
summary: A Bankless podcast interview with Paul Christiano of the Alignment Research Center on the AI alignment problem and possible solutions. It also covers his views on how an AI takeover might unfold.
why_hn: HN links it as a balanced, full-length interview with a leading alignment researcher on AI risk.

title: The Last Human – A Glimpse Into The Far Future
summary: A Kurzgesagt animation on longtermism, arguing that because the future could hold trillions of people, our actions' effect on future generations may be what matters most.
why_hn: HN uses it as a reference for the scale of future human population and long-term thinking.

title: Visualizing Data Using t-SNE
summary: A Google Tech Talk by Laurens van der Maaten, co-creator of t-SNE, on visualizing high-dimensional data by mapping it to two dimensions. It explains how the technique works and how it compares with other visualization approaches.
why_hn: HN people point to it as the canonical explanation from the method's author whenever t-SNE comes up.

title: VimSpeak Demo
summary: Ashley Feniello demonstrates VimSpeak, a voice-controlled interface for Vim inspired by Tavis Rudd's voice programming talk. The demo includes working through a VimGolf challenge by speech.
why_hn: HN mentions it as an example of voice-driven editing, and one commenter says it clarified how Vim commands compose.

title: S1E8: Show And Tell: Efrit: When Steve Gives Claude Full Access To 50 Years of Emacs Capabilities
channel: Vibe Coding With Steve and Gene
summary: Steve Yegge shows Efrit, a tool that gives Claude full control of Emacs, on the Vibe Coding with Steve and Gene show. Claude opens info pages, runs shells and even draws a Mandelbrot fractal in a buffer.
why_hn: HN shares it as a fun demo of an LLM driving a live Emacs process and orchestrating its long-standing ecosystem.

title: Someone improved my code by 40,832,277,770%
summary: Matt Parker follows the community effort to speed up his slow Wordle-solving code, which ended up running hundreds of millions of times faster. He walks through the techniques contributors used.
why_hn: Cited as a fun example of how algorithmic changes can yield enormous performance gains.

title: Freeman Dyson - Fermi's rejection of our work (94/157)
channel: Web of Stories - Life Stories of Remarkable People
summary: Freeman Dyson recounts how Enrico Fermi rejected his team's meson scattering model, noting that it had too many free parameters. It is the source of the quote about fitting an elephant.
why_hn: Cited in modeling and machine learning threads as the classic story on overfitting and justifying parameters.

title: But how do AI images and videos actually work? | Guest video by Welch Labs
summary: A guest video by Welch Labs on 3Blue1Brown explaining how text-to-image and video models work. It covers CLIP, shared embedding spaces, diffusion models (DDPM, DDIM), conditioning, guidance and negative prompts.
why_hn: HN uses it as a clear explainer for diffusion mechanics, such as negative prompts and faster sampling, and for joint text-image encoders.

title: GPT-4 Developer Livestream
summary: OpenAI's livestream demo of GPT-4 with Greg Brockman, showing its capabilities and limitations. Highlights include writing code, turning a hand-drawn sketch into a website, and a tax-question example.
why_hn: HN refers back to it as the primary source for what GPT-4 could do at launch, especially the sketch-to-website and multimodal demos.

title: Human AI is Decades Away, But We Need to Start the Debate Now | Demis Hassabis | Google Zeitgeist
summary: Demis Hassabis of DeepMind speaks at Google Zeitgeist, saying human-level AI is decades away but the debate should start now. He covers DeepMind's focus on game-playing agents.
why_hn: HN cites it for the DeepMind CEO's early views on AI and its game-playing focus, in AlphaGo and OpenAI threads.

title: First NetHack bot ascension
summary: The BotHack NetHack bot wins the game for the first time with no cheats or human intervention, in a run lasting about 3.5 hours. The description links the source code and the dumplog.
why_hn: Linked as the canonical video of the first fully automatic NetHack bot ascension in threads on NetHack and game-playing AI.

title: Building the Software 2 0 Stack (Andrej Karpathy)
summary: Andrej Karpathy's Databricks talk on Software 2.0, the shift from human-written code to code produced by neural network training. It covers how developer work moves toward curating datasets, the advantages and challenges, and opportunities for new tooling.
why_hn: HN uses it as the primary source for the 'Software 2.0' idea and recommends it as a quick talk on the next software stack.
